title: VS-05 Statistical Product Composition
text:
Applying This to Your NSO

Maturity Assessment Checklist
Use this checklist to assess your NSO’s maturity across all four process types — not just execution.
Design Maturity

Do we have documented product specifications with their component outputs and selection rules?
Do we have formal composite-indicator and time-series construction specifications?
Do we have documented internal-consistency and coherence checks with tolerances?
Do we have content templates and an editorial-review policy for interpretive content?
Do we have an approval, confidentiality, and product-versioning policy defined before composition begins?

Implementation Maturity

Are our composition engines built from design specifications (not ad-hoc spreadsheets)?
Do composites carry an uncertainty measure derived from their components?
Can a product be reproduced identically from its component versions plus the composition method?
Is the approval workflow and versioning store implemented and tamper-evident?
Do we have a formal testing process (technical, coherence, reproducibility)?

Execution Maturity

Do we select pinned component output versions and carry their accuracy metadata forward?
Do we construct composites without re-estimating component outputs?
Do we run internal-consistency and coherence checks and explain discrepancies?
Do we produce reviewed interpretive content consistent with the data and its caveats?
Do we approve and register every product as an immutable version with full lineage?

Management Maturity

Do we track KPIs (coherence pass rate, approval iterations, reproducibility) across cycles?
Do we assess coherence and interpretability of products?
Do we govern product/version lifecycles and the product-version store?
Do we produce reproducibility-audit, approval/confidentiality, and standards-compliance reports?
Do we have a formal improvement process that feeds back into design?



End-to-End Scenarios
Each scenario walks through all four process types, demonstrating how the governance pattern works in practice.

Scenario A: Labour Market Quarterly Publication
Design Phase: Product managers specify the quarterly labour-market publication: employment and unemployment rates (national and NUTS-2), a vacancy indicator, narrative, and a regional visualization, drawing on the validated LFS and administrative outputs. Coherence checks against prior quarters and the approval workflow are designed.
Implementation Phase: Engineers configure the integration engine (pinned LFS/administrative outputs), the time-series engine for the headline series, coherence checks vs. prior quarters, and the content/approval tooling. Coherence and reproducibility tests pass on historical data.
Execution Phase: For Q3-2026, an Output Data Registered event arrives. The team integrates the pinned OD-LFS-2026Q3 outputs (carrying their CIs), constructs the seasonally-relevant series, and runs coherence checks (all reconcile; coherent with Q2). The commentary explains the 0.3pp employment-rate rise and notes its significance; visualizations are produced and editorially reviewed. The product is approved and registered as an immutable version with full lineage; VS-06.0 is notified.
Management Phase: Coherence-check pass rate is 100%, approval completed in one iteration, all component CIs correctly propagated. Improvement recommendation: add an automated check comparing the vacancy indicator to a related administrative series. Recommendations fed back to design.


Scenario B: Structural Business Statistics Composite Product
Design Phase: The composite SBS product is specified to integrate the register-based and survey-based turnover/employment estimates for the same NACE × region domains, with internal-consistency checks (domains sum to totals) and coherence vs. national-accounts inputs.
Implementation Phase: Engineers configure integration of the pinned OD-BUS outputs, the consistency checks, and dominance-aware confidentiality validation for the composite. Coherence and reproducibility tests pass.
Execution Phase: Q3-2026: an Output Data Registered event arrives. The register- and survey-based components are integrated for overlapping domains; NACE-class turnover sums to the published total; the components agree within tolerance except one domain, which is returned to VS-04 for review rather than adjusted. Once resolved, the product is approved and registered (SP-BUS-2026Q3-001) with lineage to its components; VS-06.0 is notified.
Management Phase: One coherence discrepancy this cycle (resolved upstream); component reuse rate high; reproducibility audit passes. Improvement recommendation: tighten the tolerance for the recurring domain and document the reconciliation. Recommendations fed back to design.


Scenario C: Consumer Price Index Product
Design Phase: The CPI product is specified to compose the headline all-items index and main divisions from the validated item indices, with chaining/rebasing rules, coherence checks against the prior month and year, and analytical commentary.
Implementation Phase: Engineers configure the index-composition engine (designed weights and chaining), coherence checks, and the commentary/approval tooling. Coherence and reproducibility tests pass; the composed headline matches the expected value on test data.
Execution Phase: For the monthly run, an Output Data Registered event arrives with the validated item indices. The headline and division indices are composed with the period weights, coherence checks confirm consistency with the prior month and year, and the commentary explains the main contributors to the monthly change. The product is approved and registered with full lineage; VS-06.0 is notified.
Management Phase: Coherence pass rate 100%, headline reproducible from item indices + weights, approval in one iteration. Improvement recommendation: enhance the contributions visualization for the commentary. Recommendations fed back to design.

title: VS-09 Infrastructure and Platform Enablement
text:
VS-09.0 provides the technical and digital foundation that supports every part of the statistical organization. Where the other streams focus on data, methods, or governance, this one ensures all of those activities can actually run — safely, efficiently, and at scale. It delivers the IT environments, data platforms, tools, and integration services that make statistical production possible from collection to dissemination, keeping systems secure, resilient, and compliant while remaining flexible enough to adopt new technologies. The value it creates is reliable enablement — turning infrastructure from a background function into an active enabler of the statistical mission.
This document is the business-layer view of that enablement (the capability of providing platforms and services). The detailed application and technology architecture is the subject of the SAF’s application and technology layers.

Plan — understand what is needed. The lifecycle begins by defining digital and technical requirements (09.1): identifying the infrastructure needs arising from business capabilities, data volumes, and analytical complexity across the streams. These feed the design of the platform and infrastructure architecture (09.2): blueprints for data storage, processing, integration, and secure access (data fabric, data market, compute platforms).
Build — stand it up. The architecture is realized by provisioning and configuring platforms (09.3): deploying environments (on-premise, hybrid, or cloud) with the necessary governance, monitoring, and security controls, and by enabling integration and orchestration services (09.4): the APIs, workflow engines, and automation that connect the business services and processes — including the steady-state event interfaces the primary streams rely on.
Operate — keep it running and safe. Day to day, VS-09 ensures performance, security, and continuity (09.5): monitoring platform performance, implementing data protection, managing incidents, and guaranteeing availability and disaster recovery — the assurance that the whole chain can run reliably.
Improve — modernize. Finally it evolves and modernizes the technical ecosystem (09.6): introducing new technologies (often transferred from VS-08), retiring obsolete components, and keeping the foundation flexible for new data sources and operating models.

text:
Business Objects / Artefacts
VS-09 manages enabling artefacts: technical requirements, architecture blueprints, provisioned environments and platforms, integration/orchestration services and event interfaces, monitoring/security/continuity controls, and the modernization roadmap. These underpin every stream and are managed across their lifecycle (SAF-P03), with security and continuity (SAF-P10/P06) built in. Each artefact has a designated owner; changes are tracked, prior versions remain identifiable, and obsolete components are formally retired.

title: VS-09 Infrastructure and Platform Enablement
text:
Applying This to Your NSO

Maturity Assessment Checklist

Do we derive infrastructure requirements from business capabilities and data volumes (not ad-hoc)?
Do we have architecture blueprints for storage, processing, integration, and secure access?
Are environments provisioned with governance, monitoring, and security controls built in?
Do we provide integration/orchestration and the event interfaces the streams rely on?
Do we monitor performance, manage incidents, and guarantee availability and disaster recovery?
Is there a modernization path that adopts new technology (often from VS-08) and retires the obsolete?



Scenarios
Scenario A — Onboarding a secure research environment. VS-06 needs to release de-identified microdata to accredited researchers. VS-09 captures the requirement (09.1), designs the SRE architecture (09.2), provisions it with access controls and output checking (09.3/09.4), and assures its security and availability (09.5) under VS-07’s policy — so VS-06 can deliver controlled microdata access reliably.
Scenario B — Adopting a cloud processing platform. VS-08 validates a scalable processing technology. VS-09 designs and provisions the platform (09.2/09.3), enables integration with the existing pipelines (09.4), assures performance and continuity (09.5), and folds it into the modernization roadmap (09.6), so the production streams gain capacity without disruption.
Scenario C — Scaling for the census peak. The census (VS-01) will multiply ingestion and processing volumes for three months. VS-09 derives the peak requirements with the census team (09.1), updates the capacity plan and architecture (09.2), provisions elastic compute and storage ahead of the field period (09.3), and load-tests the ingestion event interfaces end to end (09.4). During the peak it monitors throughput and availability against the agreed service levels (09.5); afterwards the surge capacity is released and the lessons feed the modernization roadmap (09.6). The chain experiences the census as business as usual.

title: SAF in Brief
text: The Statistical Architecture Framework in ten minutes: what it is, the two ideas at its core, what it gives you, and what it asks of you.

title: SAF in Brief
text:
Why SAF
Statistical organisations share a need: production must remain credible, secure and efficient while adapting to new data sources, new user expectations and tighter constraints. The Statistical Architecture Framework (SAF) gives national statistical offices (NSOs) a common architectural foundation for making those changes in a controlled and coherent way.
SAF builds on earlier work, the Common Statistical Production Architecture (CSPA) and the Common Statistical Data Architecture (CSDA). It shares their aims of common understanding across organisations, interoperability, reuse and standard building blocks, but moves the emphasis from description towards implementation. It is meant to be used directly in programmes and projects, to guide actual design and implementation choices.
It does not compete with the standards an office already uses: GSBPM, GAMSO and GSIM remain as they are. SAF supplies the connecting tissue between them, linking strategy, capabilities and processes to services and technology.






ImportantA mapping framework, not an operating model



“SAF does not prescribe a single operating model, a single technology stack, or a single organisational design. It recognises that NSOs differ in mandate, maturity, and context. Instead, it provides a shared architectural foundation that can be adapted to local realities while remaining comparable across organisations.” (SAF Framework, Definition of Scope)

title: SAF in Brief
section: The two ideas at its core
text:
The two ideas at its core
Much of SAF (the motivation layer, the GAMSO-derived capability model, the ten value streams) will look familiar to anyone who knows the UNECE standards. SAF complements those standards with two further ideas, and applying the framework depends mainly on them. Neither is entirely new: steady states in particular were discussed in the statistical community before SAF gave them a formal definition.

Steady states of data
Statistical production is split into six stages, called value streams and numbered VS-01 to VS-06. Each adds one particular kind of value to the data, and each works independently of the others (they are loosely coupled, in architecture terms).
The streams exchange data at defined points called steady states. A steady state is a dataset that has reached a known quality, has been given a version and an identifier, and is available for the next stage to pick up. One stream produces it and the next consumes it, and neither needs to know more about how the other works inside.
When a stream finishes a dataset it registers it: it records the dataset in a catalogue with its identifier and a description of what was done to it. The registration sends an event telling the next stream that new data is ready, so the next stream does not have to ask.






Note“Registered” does not mean a statistical register



In the context of SAF, registering a dataset means cataloguing it so that others, inside or outside the NSO, can find and cite the exact version. It has nothing to do with a statistical register such as a business register or a population register. Both meanings appear in these documents, and the Glossary distinguishes them.



The steady states of data

The four-process governance pattern
Every stream is described through the same four process types. They form a repeating cycle rather than a one-off sequence, and each produces a different kind of result:

Design: decide how the work should be done (rules, methodology, specifications, policies). Provides metadata.
Implementation: build, configure and test the systems that will do it. Provides the execution process.
Execution: run the work each production cycle. Provides the statistical data.
Management: check quality, monitor performance and feed improvements back to Design. Provides quality reports.

TipFor GSBPM readers



Design maps to Phase 2, Implementation to Phase 3, Execution to Phases 4–7 as appropriate to the domain, and Management to the overarching Quality Management / Phase 8. Separating the four lets an office change how a stream is built without touching how it is designed, and govern quality without owning execution.

title: SAF in Brief
text:
How the pieces fit
Six primary streams form the production chain. Four supporting streams (VS-07 Governance & Compliance, VS-08 Innovation & Methodological Development, VS-09 Infrastructure & Platform Enablement, VS-10 Customer & Stakeholder Engagement) enable and constrain all six continuously. They have no steady-state transition of their own. They run as a plan → build → operate → improve cycle, produce enabling capabilities rather than data, and align to GAMSO rather than GSBPM.

The last column names each stream’s signature discipline: the rule that defines it, stating what the stream must always do or must never do.
Beneath the streams sit the capability model (70 capabilities in four groups, taken from GAMSO 1.2) and the motivation layer (drivers, goals, principles, outcomes, stakeholders), which give the framework its vocabulary and basis. The streams and steady states are where they are applied.






Caution

title: SAF in Brief
text:
What adopting SAF gives you
The framework names six outcomes for an office that adopts it: accelerated modernization, enhanced data quality, improved interoperability, improved trust and transparency, increased efficiency, and a shared knowledge base for the organisation and its partners.
In practice these follow from the steady states:

State #2 puts data from different sources into common formats and classifications, so datasets can be combined and reused across products. This matters more as survey response rates fall and offices combine surveys with administrative sources to produce multi-source statistics.
State #3 is designed for reuse, so the same processing is not repeated by each unit.
Loose coupling means one capability, such as a collection channel, an editing engine or a dissemination platform, can be modernised without disrupting the rest of the chain.
Every dataset carries its lineage (the trace back through each step to the data it came from) together with its quality documentation, so an office can show how any published figure was produced.

For NSOs this means lower risk, more agility, and better alignment between IT and business objectives. For international organisations it means harmonisation and comparability. For citizens and policymakers it means statistics whose trustworthiness can be demonstrated.

title: SAF in Brief
text:
What it commits you to
Adopting the steady-state model comes with concrete obligations, and loose coupling only works in practice if they are met.






ImportantAdopting SAF means you commit to




Naming what is handed over at every boundary. Streams exchange finished, registered datasets (artefacts, in SAF’s vocabulary) with their metadata, never internal working data. Neither side then needs to know how the other works inside (SAF-P07).
A catalogue. Every artefact is identified, versioned and catalogued. Once registered, it is available to authorised users in the office and, where agreements allow, to partners across the national statistical system, so collection, cleaning and analysis are not duplicated (SAF-P08).
Metadata from the start. Every artefact carries its provenance, method, accuracy, classification and lineage, recorded when each value is created or changed rather than reconstructed months later (SAF-P09). Many offices have their best metadata at dissemination today; building it up from ingestion onwards is often the largest investment SAF asks for.
An owner and quality criteria for each state. Someone, often called a data steward, is accountable for each state, and a dataset must meet explicit criteria to be in that state.
Security built in. Access control, integrity checks and tamper-evident audit trails are part of every pipeline from the start (SAF-P10).
Confidentiality at several points. Direct identifiers are removed or pseudonymised at standardisation (#2) at the latest, and earlier where that suits the process. Disclosure risk is assessed on enrichment (#3), disclosure control is applied to outputs (#4), and a final disclosure check comes before release (#5); nothing is released until it passes (SAF-P11). Other methods, such as input privacy for data integration, synthetic data or differential privacy, can also be used.
Design and management of artefacts, as well as execution. Rules, methods and specifications exist and are versioned (for example in a Git repository) before a cycle runs; quality reports and improvement recommendations feed back into design afterwards.
Events. A handover is announced by a registration event, so the next stream does not have to ask.
Open tooling where it carries statistical method. Methods that produce official figures are built on shared, open components, and improvements are contributed back, so the statistical community keeps collective control of them instead of depending on a vendor (SAF-P01). See Open Source in SAF.



Registered artefacts are also immutable: they are not changed once registered. A correction produces a new version instead of overwriting the old one, which makes it possible, years later, to show the data behind a published figure.
None of these commitments prescribes how you meet it. A boundary is an agreement between streams and does not have to match an organisational unit: one team may own several states, and a central unit may run processing for many domains. SAF only requires that the agreement exists and is written down.
Nor does every process have to pass through all six states. A process that builds on data another team has already registered (macro statistics built on shared Processed Data, for example) starts from that data without creating earlier artefacts. When nothing changes between two states, as can happen between #4 and #5, one artefact can serve both. When a step uses data without changing its values, a logged event pointing to the existing version is enough for lineage. In each case the choice is recorded in the catalogue: comply or explain. These rules are set out in Applying the steady states pragmatically.

text: A beginner’s guide. Two processes are followed from start to finish through the steady states, and an exercise helps you map one of your own production processes onto the framework.

title: Getting Started with SAF
text:
1. Key concepts

Value stream: a sequence of steps that together create a statistical output. Think of it as a production line: VS-01 to VS-06 each add a specific kind of value to the data.
Value stream stage vs. business process: the stage (VS-0x.y) says what value is added; the business process describes how your office actually does it. The numbering maps one-to-one, so this guide uses VS-0x.y for both.
Steady state: a fixed handover point, where a versioned, quality-assured dataset produced by one stream is consumed by the next. The states are numbered from #0 (source data, still at the provider) to #6 (data in users’ hands).
The four process types: every stream is described through the same four groups: Design (decide how it should work), Implementation (build and test it), Execution (run it each production cycle) and Management (check quality and feed improvements back).
Business service / object / event: what a stream offers to others / the data it works on / the signals streams send each other (for example “Raw Data Registered” tells the next stream new data is ready).
Artefact: what is handed over at a steady state, meaning the dataset plus the metadata describing it. It is immutable: a correction never overwrites a registered artefact but creates a new version. To register an artefact is to catalogue it with an identifier so others can find and cite that exact version. This has nothing to do with a statistical register such as the business or population register.

title: Getting Started with SAF
section: 3. The walk, one state at a time
text:
3. The walk, one state at a time
Each state below is one handover card: what arrives, what the stream does, what it deliberately does not do, what it registers, the event it fires, the metadata that travels, and how the two threads differ. The event and metadata rows have the same shape on every card. This is deliberate: a stream only needs to understand that shape, not the work of the stream before it. The cards show each stream’s Execution process; section 4 shows the three other process types around it.

State #1 — Raw Data (VS-01 Data Acquisition and Ingestion)
Source Data → #1 Raw Data. Received into NSO custody in original form, with provenance and basic validation. Nothing about the content is changed here.


State #1 handover card








Labour Force Survey
Tax register → business statistics




What arrives
Survey responses from the sampled households: CAWI first, CATI follow-up after two weeks, CAPI for hard-to-reach cases. Trigger: survey response submitted.
The Q3 quarterly file, delivered via SFTP on day 38 of the 45-day SLA. Before the window opened, the team verified the SLA (≥ 98% of expected records), confirmed the SFTP credentials, and recorded the active agreement reference. Trigger: delivery received.


What this stream does
Confirms the round’s needs and sources; activates the legal basis; runs each mode, capturing ingestion metadata at receipt (mode, completion date, instrument version); validates completeness and structure per return; logs every result.
The automated pipeline fires on arrival: XSD valid, SHA-256 checksum matches the manifest, virus scan clean, 2,347,891 records (99.2% of expected, above the 98% threshold); 14 corporate IDs not in the business register are flagged but not rejected (known register lag).


What is not done here
No coding, editing or change of values: the content is what the respondent gave.
No pseudonymisation (deferred to VS-02 by agreement); no conversion of amounts; the XML is kept as received.


What is registered
RD-LFS-2026Q3-001: the ~42,000 returns in original form, with per-return provenance and a completeness score.
RD-TAX-2026Q3-001: the file in original XML, with provenance, a quality assessment (completeness 99.2%, timeliness on time, conformance pass with 14 flags), and the agreement reference.


Event fired → who listens
“Raw Data Registered” → VS-02
“Raw Data Registered” → VS-02


Metadata that travels (both)
Provenance, source, collection method, receipt timestamp, file hash, agreement reference, quality assessment (completeness, timeliness, conformance), and a BIV classification (a security label covering availability, integrity and confidentiality; the letters come from the Dutch).



What differs
Primary collection: the NSO designed the instrument and runs the fieldwork; the raw artefact is many submissions across several modes.
Secondary collection: the NSO negotiated an SLA and receives one file; validation is entirely automated. The contract at the boundary is identical.










NoteSignature discipline — no data without metadata



Every dataset is enriched at ingestion with provenance, source, method, timestamp, a quality assessment and a BIV classification, as SAF-P09 requires, with security and privacy built in from the start (SAF-P10/P11).








NoteIn the main document



Full chapter: VS-01 Data Acquisition and Ingestion. Its Steady State Transition, Boundary Interface Specifications and End-to-End Scenarios go further than the card above. Note that the survey scenario there is a Household Budget Survey; the LFS thread above is built from the LFS design example in the same chapter. A one-page summary of this stream also sits in Business Architecture.




State #2 — Standardized Data (VS-02 Data Standardization and Integration)
#1 Raw → #2 Standardized. Aligned to common structure, format, and classifications, with values unchanged. This is the first point at which data from different domains can be combined.


State #2 handover card








Labour Force Survey
Tax register → business statistics




What arrives
“Raw Data Registered” for RD-LFS-2026Q3-001, ~42,000 returns.
“Raw Data Registered” for RD-TAX-2026Q3-001, 2,347,891 records.


What this stream does
Converts the file into the target structure; maps education codes one-to-one to ISCED-2011 and region codes to NUTS-3 via correspondence tables; records the survey’s employment-status definition difference from ILO as metadata; pseudonymises the personal identifier. Conformance validation passes, including the no-loss-of-content check (42,000 records, no value changed).
Maps the tax authority’s internal activity codes to NACE Rev. 2 (99.4% coverage); converts the XML into the target structure; attaches the statistical business register (SBR) key; records that turnover is in thousands of EUR on a fiscal-year basis as metadata; values are left exactly as received. 14 records without an SBR match are flagged but retained. Conformance passes with every value unchanged.


What is not done here
The 42,000 free-text occupation strings are not coded; they are flagged and handed to VS-03 for ISCO-08 coding. The definition difference is not reconciled.
Turnover is not converted to units or to a calendar year; the 0.6% of activity codes with no correspondence are flagged for VS-03.


What is registered
SD-LFS-2026Q3-001, with mapping lineage to the raw artefact.
SD-BUS-2026Q3-001, with lineage to RD-TAX-2026Q3-001 and a note that unit/period conversion remains to be done.


Event fired → who listens
“Standardized Data Registered” → VS-03
“Standardized Data Registered” → VS-03


Metadata that travels (both)
Source-to-target mapping lineage, applied classification scheme versions, recorded unit/currency/reference-period bases, the list of unmapped or uncoded values for VS-03 to code, definition-difference records, conformance assessment, pseudonymisation record, BIV classification.



What differs
Deterministic mapping of coded answers; pseudonymisation of persons.
Mapping of an administrative code list to NACE; linkage key attached; the bases of amounts recorded so a later stream can convert them.




Confidentiality step at this state: direct identifiers are replaced by pseudonymous keys before the artefact is registered.






NoteSignature discipline — standardization without loss of content



VS-02 only maps codes one-to-one, reformats the structure, and adds metadata. It never changes a value. Recoding through a fixed correspondence table counts as standardisation because the meaning of the value stays the same. Unit/currency conversion, reference-period alignment, value reconciliation and interpretive free-text coding are left to VS-03.








NoteIn the main document



Full chapter: VS-02 Data Standardization and Integration. See its Steady State Transition, Boundary Interface Specifications and End-to-End Scenarios: Scenario A is the LFS, Scenario B the tax register. A one-page summary of this stream also sits in Business Architecture.




State #3 — Processed Data (VS-03 Data Editing and Enrichment)
#2 Standardized → #3 Processed. Content validated, edited, imputed, enriched, integrated; derived variables added. This is the only stream that deliberately changes values, and every change must be documented and reversible.


State #3 handover card








Labour Force Survey
Tax register → business statistics




What arrives
“Standardized Data Registered” for SD-LFS-2026Q3-001, plus the flagged occupation strings and the recorded definition difference.
“Standardized Data Registered” for SD-BUS-2026Q3-001, plus the recorded unit and fiscal-year bases and the unmapped activity codes.


What this stream does
Error detection flags inconsistencies and outliers; auto-corrections are applied and high-impact records adjudicated. The 42,000 occupations are coded to ISCO-08 (88% auto-coded, the rest computer-assisted and reviewed). Income non-response (9%) is imputed and flagged. Employment status is harmonised to the ILO definition under the reconciliation rule.
Outliers and duplicates are detected and corrected with full lineage. Turnover is converted to units on a calendar-year basis (conversion factor and original value stored). The tax data and the structural business survey are integrated on the SBR key, with the reconciliation rule applied where they disagree. Turnover-per-employee is derived.


What is not done here
No weighting or estimation: no statistics are computed here. Observed values are never overwritten: the original is kept beside every edit, and imputed values stay distinguishable.
Same. Integration does not silently pick one source over the other: reconciliation follows a designed rule and is logged.


What is registered
PD-LFS-2026Q3-001: an immutable quality version with complete edit lineage.
PD-BUS-2026Q3-001, with lineage to SD-BUS-2026Q3-001.


Event fired → who listens
“Processed Data Registered” → VS-04
“Processed Data Registered” → VS-04


Metadata that travels (both)
Edit lineage (original value, rule, reason), imputation flags and methods, derived-variable formulae and classification, integration/linkage lineage, quality-improvement assessment, quality-version identifier, BIV classification.



What differs
Interpretive coding and imputation of item non-response dominate.
Conversion, multi-source integration, and derivation dominate. In both, every change is traceable to its original value.




Confidentiality step at this state: disclosure risk is assessed on enrichment and linkage. In the tax thread, the disclosure-risk report confirms the survey–register linkage stays within assessed bounds.






NoteSignature discipline — full traceability



VS-03 is the domain that changes values, under the guarantee of no undocumented or irreversible change: original values are preserved beside edited ones, imputations are flagged, and every version is reproducible.








NoteIn the main document



Full chapter: VS-03 Data Editing and Enrichment. See its Steady State Transition, Boundary Interface Specifications and End-to-End Scenarios. A one-page summary of this stream also sits in Business Architecture.




State #4a — Statistics (Output Data): analytical outputs (VS-04 Estimation, Analysis, and Statistical Modeling)
#3 Processed → #4 Statistics. The microdata is not edited further; statistics are computed from it, each with a measure of its accuracy, and disclosure control is applied to the outputs.


State #4a handover card








Labour Force Survey
Tax register → business statistics




What arrives
“Processed Data Registered” for PD-LFS-2026Q3-001, with its imputation flags.
“Processed Data Registered” for PD-BUS-2026Q3-001, the integrated business dataset.


What this stream does
Confirms the pre-approved approach and current calibration totals. Calibration converges and the weighted margins reproduce the population register. The employment rate is estimated at 71.4% (95% CI ± 0.5 pp nationally, wider at NUTS-2), with variance inflated for the imputed values. Coherence checks against Q2 pass. Small NUTS-2 cells are suppressed.
Aggregates are computed by NACE × region. Unstable small domains are estimated with a small-area model and flagged distinctly from direct aggregates. Dominant-unit cells are suppressed. Coherence with national-accounts inputs is checked.


What is not done here
No microdata is changed. No product is assembled or published.
Same. Model-based estimates are never presented as if they were direct aggregates.


What is registered
OD-LFS-2026Q3: the output version with methodology, weights, and accuracy attached.
OD-BUS-2026Q3-001, with methodology and accuracy, linked to PD-BUS-2026Q3-001.


Event fired → who listens
“Output Data Registered” → VS-05
“Output Data Registered” → VS-05


Metadata that travels (both)
Methodology and parameters, weights, accuracy measures (sampling error, confidence intervals), model diagnostics, applied disclosure-control record, quality indicators, output-version identifier, lineage to the processed source, BIV classification.



What differs
Design-based estimation with calibration to register totals; the variance reflects both the survey design and VS-03’s imputation.
Register-based aggregation plus a small-area model for thin domains; disclosure control is about dominant units rather than small cells. In both, every figure carries the method and accuracy that produced it and can be regenerated.




Confidentiality step at this state: statistical disclosure control is applied to the outputs, so that they could be released.






NoteSignature discipline — methodological transparency



Every estimate carries the method, parameters, and accuracy measure that produced it and can be regenerated; imputation uncertainty from VS-03 is reflected in the variance, and disclosure control is applied to the outputs so that they could be released.








NoteIn the main document



Full chapter: VS-04 Estimation, Analysis, and Statistical Modeling. See its Steady State Transition, Boundary Interface Specifications and End-to-End Scenarios. A one-page summary of this stream also sits in Business Architecture.




State #4b — Statistics (Output Data): approved product (VS-05 Statistical Product Composition)
Still within State #4. The framework has a single State #4; #4a / #4b is this guide’s shorthand for its two halves, because two different streams work on it. VS-04 produced individual validated estimates, and VS-05 now assembles them into an approved product that readers can use. The numbers themselves do not change.


State #4b handover card








Labour Force Survey
Tax register → business statistics




What arrives
“Output Data Registered” for OD-LFS-2026Q3.
“Output Data Registered” for OD-BUS-2026Q3-001.


What this stream does
Integrates the pinned OD-LFS-2026Q3 employment and unemployment outputs (national and NUTS-2) and the latest administrative vacancy output, carrying their confidence intervals; constructs the headline series; runs coherence checks (all reconcile; coherent with Q2). The commentary explains the 0.3 pp rise in the employment rate and notes its significance; visualisations are editorially reviewed.
Integrates the register-based and survey-based turnover and employment estimates for the same NACE × region domains. NACE-class turnover sums to the published total. The components agree within tolerance except one domain, which is returned to VS-04 for review rather than adjusted.


What is not done here
Nothing is re-estimated. Discrepancies are explained or sent back, never quietly adjusted.
Same.


What is registered
SP-LFS-2026Q3-001: the approved quarterly labour-market product, an immutable version with full lineage to its components.
SP-BUS-2026Q3-001, once the returned domain is resolved, with lineage to its components.


Event fired → who listens
“Statistical Product Registered” → VS-06
“Statistical Product Registered” → VS-06


Metadata that travels (both)
Component lineage, composition/indicator method, propagated accuracy, coherence results, interpretive content, approval record, confidentiality status, product-version identifier, BIV classification.



What differs
Composes survey and administrative outputs into a publication with narrative.
Composes register- and survey-based estimates into a structural business statistics composite. In both, component versions are pinned and approval precedes registration.




Confidentiality step at this state: the product is validated against dissemination and confidentiality standards before it is approved.






NoteSignature discipline — coherence and interpretability



VS-05 composes validated outputs (it does not re-estimate). Products are internally consistent, coherent with related and prior statistics, carry their components’ accuracy metadata, and are approved against dissemination and confidentiality standards before being registered.








NoteIn the main document



Full chapter: VS-05 Statistical Product Composition. Its Steady State Transition explains why State #4 has two halves. A one-page summary of this stream also sits in Business Architecture.




State #5 — Released Data, then #6 Consumed Data (VS-06 Dissemination and Service Delivery)
#4 Approved product → #5 Released → #6 Consumed. This is where data leaves the office. The key control is a final disclosure check, and nothing is released until it is passed. VS-06 does not alter the statistics; it protects, formats and delivers them.


State #5 handover card








Labour Force Survey
Tax register → business statistics




What arrives
“Statistical Product Registered” for the Q3-2026 labour-market product.
“Statistical Product Registered” for the SBS product.


What this stream does
Confirms the plan; applies final disclosure control (two small NUTS-2 cells suppressed); clears the disclosure-risk gate. At 09:00 the figures publish simultaneously on the website, the API, and the dashboard; embargoed media publish at the same moment. Documentation and methodology notes accompany the release; the helpdesk handles queries; usage and feedback are collected.
Aggregate tables are disclosure-controlled and published openly. The microdata is de-identified to the agreed standard and made available in a secure research environment (SRE) for accredited researchers, who are onboarded with the data dictionary and methodology. The helpdesk performs output-checking so that results researchers export also meet disclosure rules. SRE usage is logged.


What is not done here
No figure is changed. No release before the gate is passed; no privileged early sight outside policy.
Same. Researchers work inside the environment; nothing leaves without output-checking.


What is registered
The release version, with lineage to SP-LFS-2026Q3-001.
The release version, with lineage to SP-BUS-2026Q3-001.


Event fired → who listens
“Statistics Released” → users and society; feedback returns to VS-06.5 and VS-10.
“Statistics Released” → users and researchers; feedback returns to VS-06.5 and VS-10.


Metadata that travels (both)
Final disclosure-control record, documentation/methodology notes, reference and structural metadata, channel/format, release timestamp, release-version identifier, lineage to the approved product.



What differs
An open aggregate release at a fixed minute, with equal access enforced.
Open tables plus controlled microdata access with output checking. The gate is the same; the channels are not.




Confidentiality step at this state: the final disclosure-control gate. Once released, the data is Consumed Data (#6), used by external parties for their own purposes, outside the NSO’s direct control. The documentation delivered at #5 supports appropriate use at #6.
In some processes nothing changes between the approved product and the release. A proposal under review allows the #4 artefact to be marked as released in that case, instead of being registered again, provided the release steps are still carried out and recorded. See Applying the steady states pragmatically.






NoteSignature discipline — accessibility, trust, and the release gate



Accurate, timely, understandable delivery through secure channels, gated by final statistical disclosure control (no release without confidentiality clearance) and supported by documentation that enables responsible, equal-access use. VS-06 relies on the supporting streams VS-07 (compliance), VS-09 (platforms), and VS-10 (user needs).








NoteIn the main document



Full chapter: VS-06 Dissemination and Service Delivery. See its Steady State Transition, Boundary Interface Specifications and End-to-End Scenarios. A one-page summary of this stream also sits in Business Architecture.

section: 4. The other three process types, worked once
text:
4. The other three process types, worked once
The cards above show the Execution process of each stream, which runs every production cycle. Around it, three other process types run in every stream: Design decides how the work should be done and provides the metadata; Implementation builds and tests the systems and provides the execution process; Management checks quality and performance and feeds improvements back to Design. The cycle looks the same in every stream, so it is worked here once, for the tax thread at State #1.






flowchart LR
    D["**Design**
    _metadata_"] -->|"guides building"| I["**Implement**
    _execution process_"]
    I -->|"production-ready"| E["**Execute**
    _statistical data_"]
    E -->|"data & process logs"| M["**Manage**
    _quality reports_"]
    M -->|"improvement feedback"| D

    style D fill:#7c3aed,color:#fff,stroke:#6d28d9
    style I fill:#2563eb,color:#fff,stroke:#1d4ed8
    style E fill:#059669,color:#fff,stroke:#047857
    style M fill:#d97706,color:#fff,stroke:#b45309




Figure 4: The four-process governance pattern. Each of the six primary streams runs this full cycle; the feedback arrow from Management to Design closes the loop.





Design. Statistical designers define the data requirement: quarterly corporate income-tax declarations for all legal entities, for use in national accounts and business statistics. The data model maps the tax authority’s XML schema to the NSO’s raw-data structure: 47 fields retained, 12 derived, the corporate ID as the linkage key. The SLA is set at delivery within 45 calendar days of quarter end, at least 98% of expected records, in XML with XSD validation. Validation rules cover schema validation, referential integrity of the corporate ID against the business register, and amount fields within historical range. The privacy framework records that data is received under the statistics-act mandate, with pseudonymisation deferred to VS-02 by agreement.
Implementation. System configurators set up a dedicated secure file-transfer endpoint, locked down so that only the tax authority’s systems can connect to it. Data engineers configure automated ingestion: file arrival triggers the validation pipeline (XSD check, checksum, virus scan, completeness, referential integrity, range check). Metadata registration is automated: on successful validation a provenance record is created and linked to the agreement, and quality scores are calculated and stored. The pipeline is tested by resubmitting Q1-2026 historical data; one false-positive range check is found and its threshold adjusted.
Execution. This is the State #1 card above: the Q3 file arrives on day 38, the pipeline validates it, RD-TAX-2026Q3-001 is registered, and “Raw Data Registered” notifies VS-02.
Management. The Q3 quality scorecard shows completeness at 99.2% (stable against Q1 = 99.1% and Q2 = 99.3%) and delivery seven days ahead of the SLA deadline. The 14 unmatched corporate IDs are all newly registered businesses, consistent with previous quarters. SLA compliance stands at 100% for 12 consecutive quarters; metadata completeness is 100%. No improvement recommendation is needed this cycle; an annual agreement-renewal review is scheduled for Q4.
Two things are worth noticing. The Design artefacts (the schema mapping, the validation rules, the SLA) existed before the first file arrived, and Execution follows them. And Management ends with a decision about Design, even when that decision is to change nothing.
What Design and Management look like in the other five streams, in one line each:

Design and Management around each stream







Stream
Design prepares
Management watches and feeds back




VS-02 Standardization
The target data model, deterministic classification correspondences, harmonisation and conformance rules, the privacy framework
Mapping coverage and the unmapped-value rate; classification versions; extensions to the correspondence tables


VS-03 Editing & Enrichment
Error-detection and editing rules with a selective-editing strategy, the imputation methodology, derivation and coding specs, integration rules, the versioning policy
Edit, imputation, and over-editing rates; quality improvement against the State #2 baseline; audit of the edit lineage


VS-04 Estimation
The estimation strategy and accuracy approach, weighting/calibration methodology, aggregation and model specifications, the validation and disclosure-control policy
Accuracy, timeliness, and revisions; coherence; reproducibility audits


VS-05 Composition
The product portfolio, composite-indicator specs, coherence checks, content templates, the approval/confidentiality/versioning framework
Coherence-check pass rates and approval iterations; product quality; reproducibility and approval audits


VS-06 Dissemination
The dissemination and access strategy, final disclosure-control and de-identification rules, channel/format/documentation standards, release governance
Punctuality, usage, and satisfaction; accessibility; disclosure and equal-access compliance, with VS-07

5. Map your own process
The framework is explicit that “SAF does not prescribe a single operating model, a single technology stack, or a single organisational design”; what it gives you is a shared way of describing the one you have and the one you want. This exercise does that for one production process in three steps. Invite the people who design, build, run and monitor the process; the four process types also make a good attendance list.

Step 1 — Find your steady-state boundaries
Pick one statistical product. For each handover in the chain, answer the questions in the worksheet. Each column is one of the four things the framework says a boundary must specify (the artefact, its metadata, the event, and where responsibility transfers), phrased as a question.
Filled in for the tax thread, the worksheet reads:

Your process does not have to fill every row. If it starts from data another team has already registered, such as a shared #3, begin at that row and note the artefact you start from. If two states hold the same data, for example when nothing changes between #4 and #5, write “same artefact as #4” and give the reason. See Applying the steady states pragmatically, a proposal still under review.






TipReading your worksheet: four symptoms and what they mean




You cannot name the artefact at a handover → either the boundary does not exist yet, or two states have been merged or skipped. Both can be legitimate if you can explain why. If you cannot, deciding where the boundary belongs is your first architecture decision.
The next team has to read the previous team’s code, or ask them how to use the data → the streams are tightly coupled (SAF-P07). The metadata that should travel with the artefact is living in people’s heads or in scripts.
The same data is re-collected or re-cleaned by a second team → the artefact is not shared property (SAF-P08). This is usually a problem of registration or discovery rather than a technical one.
Values change between #1 and #2 → the standardisation boundary is in the wrong place. Anything that changes a value belongs in VS-03, where every change is logged against its original.

A boundary is an agreement between streams and does not have to match an organisational unit. One team may own several states, and a central unit may run processing for many domains. The agreement in each row just needs to be written down.

TipScoring in a 90-minute workshop



Ten minutes per stream column, with the people who design, build, run, and monitor that stream in the room. Score by consensus; when the room disagrees, record the lower score and the reason. Precision matters less than the overall pattern. A common result is a stream scoring 2 on Execution but 0 on Design and Management: it runs well, but without design or management artefacts it cannot be changed safely.


Any cell scoring 0 or 1 points you at the stream’s full checklist in the SAF Framework document (the Maturity Assessment Checklist under Applying This to Your NSO in that stream’s deep dive), where twenty detailed questions describe what “systematic” looks like.

title: Statistical Architecture Framework
text:
SAF is a shared way for national statistical offices to describe how they turn data into official statistics, and to change how they do it while keeping production running.
It is written for the people who do that work: methodologists, statisticians, data and IT staff, quality and privacy officers, managers and CIOs. You do not need a background in architecture to read this site or the framework itself.

title: Statistical Architecture Framework
section: The one idea worth knowing first
text:
The one idea worth knowing first
SAF splits statistical production into stages that pass data to each other at agreed points called steady states. At each of these points the data has reached a known quality, has a version and an identifier, and comes with a description of what was done to it. The stage that picks it up does not need to know anything else about how the previous stage works.
Because of this, an office can modernise one part of its production (a collection channel, an editing engine, a publication platform) without disrupting the others. It can also show how any published figure was produced.
The formal model behind all of this is available in ArchiMate format.

title: Glossary
text:
Words SAF uses that are not everyday statistical vocabulary, explained without assuming a background in architecture. Where a term means something different inside SAF than elsewhere in a statistical office, the entry says so.
Artefact: what is handed over at a boundary, meaning a dataset or file together with the metadata that describes it. SAF says “artefact” rather than “dataset” because the metadata is part of what is handed over.
BIV classification: a security label recording how sensitive a dataset is on three axes: availability, integrity and confidentiality. The letters come from the Dutch (Beschikbaarheid, Integriteit, Vertrouwelijkheid), which is why they do not match the English words.
Boundary: the point where one value stream hands data to the next. In SAF a boundary is an agreement between two streams and does not have to match an organisational unit. It states what is handed over, what metadata comes with it, what signals the handover, and who becomes responsible. One team may own several boundaries.
Disclosure control (SDC): statistical disclosure control, the familiar practice of suppressing, rounding or perturbing figures so that individual people or businesses cannot be identified. SAF applies it at several points: disclosure risk is assessed on enrichment (#3), disclosure control is applied to outputs (#4), and a final check is made before release (#5). Removing or pseudonymising direct identifiers is a separate privacy measure, done at standardisation (#2) at the latest and earlier where that suits the process. Other methods, such as synthetic data or differential privacy, can also protect confidentiality.
Event: a short notification a value stream publishes when it has finished something, for example “Raw Data Registered”. The next stream listens for it, so it never has to ask whether the data is ready.
Immutable: frozen. Once a dataset is registered at a steady state it is not edited in place. A correction produces a new version, so any published figure can be traced back to the exact data it came from.
Lineage: the trace from a figure back through every step to the data it came from. If a published number is questioned, lineage lets you show how it was produced. Lineage does not require a copy of the data at every step: when a step uses a dataset without changing its values, a logged record of that step pointing to the existing version is enough.
Loosely coupled: two parts of the chain work independently and exchange only finished, described datasets. Neither needs to know how the other works inside, so one part can be replaced or modernised without disturbing the rest.
Metadata: the description that travels with data: where it came from, what was done to it, by which rule or method, how accurate it is, and how it is classified.
Provenance: the record of where a dataset came from and how it arrived: the source, the collection method, when it was received, and under which agreement.
Register / registered: not a statistical register. In SAF, to register a dataset means to record it in a catalogue with an identifier and its metadata, so that others, inside the office or outside it, can find it, trust it and cite the exact version they used. A statistical register, such as the business register or the population register, is something else. Both meanings appear in these documents.
Signature discipline: a phrase used on this site for the rule that defines each value stream, stating what it must always do or must never do. VS-02’s is “change no values”. Recoding a value into a standard classification through a fixed correspondence table counts as standardisation, because the meaning of the value stays the same; interpreting free text, such as coding job titles to ISCO, is left to VS-03. VS-03’s discipline is “change values, but never invisibly”.
Steady state: a defined handover point in the production chain, where a versioned, quality-assured dataset is finished by one stream and picked up by the next. SAF numbers them from #0 (data still at the provider) to #6 (data in users’ hands). A steady state is both a place where data waits to be exchanged and a stage in the value added to it. Not every process passes through every state. A process may start from a dataset another team has already registered, and two states may share one dataset when nothing changes between them (see Applying the steady states pragmatically, a proposal under review).
Value stream: a sequence of steps that together add one particular kind of value to data. Think of a production line: VS-01 to VS-06 each add something specific, and VS-07 to VS-10 support all of them.
VS-0x.y: the numbering used for the stages of a value stream, for example VS-03.2. The same number identifies both the stage (what value is added) and the business process (how your office does it), so the two can always be matched.

title: Motivation
text:
Architecture drivers in many ocassions are the same forces that make change necessary. They capture the pressures, trends, and constraints that statistical offices face and which the SAF is designed to address. Drivers can be external, such as technological advancements or new regulations, or internal, such as the need to replace legacy systems or respond to stakeholder demands. By documenting these drivers, SAF ensures that its architecture is not an abstract ideal but a practical response to real-world challenges.
For statistical organizations, these drivers are particularly intense. Rapid technological change requires continuous adaptation, while political and societal pressures demand timely, relevant, and transparent data. At the same time, many organizations face limited budgets and must balance modernization with cost control.
Recognizing these drivers helps statistical offices prioritize investments and avoid the pitfalls of reactive decision-making, where short-term fixes can lead to long-term inefficiencies.
Including architecture drivers in the framework also strengthens communication with stakeholders. By clearly articulating the external and internal factors shaping architecture, CIOs, CTOs, and enterprise architects can build a stronger case for change, justify strategic initiatives, and ensure that all parties understand the urgency of modernization. In this way, SAF creates a shared understanding of why action is necessary and what risks are avoided by adopting a structured framework.


The environment for producing official statistics is shifting from one of isolated data collection toward a complex and interdependent data ecosystem. Traditional surveys, once the cornerstone of statistical production, now coexist with administrative, commercial, platform, and community-driven data sources. This evolution expands opportunities for collaboration but also introduces dependencies on actors, technologies, and infrastructures outside the direct control of statistical organizations.
Open-source development has become a key element of this ecosystem. It provides a shared foundation for innovation, transparency, and cost efficiency, while fostering cooperation across institutional and national boundaries. As part of a wider collaboration model, open source allows NSIs to co-develop tools and methods with peers, academia, and private partners, ensuring that advances in technology benefit the entire statistical community. SAF addresses this driver by promoting architectures that support secure data sharing, standardized interfaces, and transparent governance models. It enables NSIs to participate confidently in broader ecosystems, from national data platforms to European data spaces, where production may take place across multiple environments and jurisdictions. By combining openness with strong governance and clear accountability, SAF ensures that collaboration and shared development strengthen rather than compromise the integrity of official statistics.


Artificial intelligence, automation, and rapid technological progress are transforming how data is created, processed, and consumed. For statistical organizations, these developments bring both opportunities and dependencies. Emerging tools can automate repetitive tasks, enhance analytical capabilities, and strengthen quality assurance. At the same time, they redefine what it means for official statistics to remain relevant and trusted in an environment increasingly shaped by intelligent systems.
The accelerating pace of innovation requires statistical offices to be both adopters and enablers of AI. Internally, this means developing architectures and competencies that support automation, machine learning, and advanced analytics within secure and transparent frameworks. Externally, it requires ensuring that official statistics are AI-ready - that is, machine-readable, machine-understandable, and interoperable with the digital platforms and applications used by policymakers, researchers, and citizens.
SAF addresses this driver by enabling NSIs to adopt a risk-based approach to modernization. It supports architectures where critical processes that demand methodological rigor, transparency, and control can be tightly governed, while areas that are less sensitive can be automated to a higher degree. This balance ensures that innovation strengthens quality and efficiency without compromising security, privacy, or trust.
Through modular and standards-based design, SAF provides the flexibility needed to integrate emerging technologies at an appropriate pace. It allows NSIs to benefit from automation and AI-driven tools while maintaining full accountability for statistical quality, data protection, and institutional independence.




Trust is the foundation of official statistics. In an environment increasingly challenged by misinformation, privacy concerns, and competition from unregulated data providers, maintaining public confidence requires more than compliance. It depends on scientific rigor, transparency, and clear accountability for how data is handled and communicated.
SAF addresses this driver by embedding trust and protection directly into architectural design. It promotes governance and technical controls that safeguard confidentiality, ensure methodological integrity, and make processes traceable and transparent. Through a risk-based approach, SAF allows NSIs to apply strict oversight where sensitivity and quality demands are high, while enabling greater automation and shared solutions where risks are lower. This balance ensures that modernization strengthens trust rather than compromising it.



Statistical organizations operate in an increasingly complex and uncertain world. Global tensions, political polarization, and shifting power dynamics influence both the demand for and the perception of official statistics. At the same time, digital interdependence and cross-border data flows require statistical systems to remain open and interoperable while safeguarding national and institutional integrity.
SAF addresses this driver by providing a stable and transparent foundation for cooperation and resilience. It promotes interoperable architectures based on shared standards, enabling NSIs to exchange data and methods securely even in times of uncertainty. By embedding governance and design principles that protect independence and transparency, SAF helps organizations maintain credibility, comparability, and trust in environments where facts themselves are often contested.



Many statistical organizations face increasing expectations with limited budgets, aging systems, and challenges in recruiting and retaining specialized skills. At the same time, the demand for more timely, detailed, and multidomain outputs continues to grow. Meeting these needs requires not only efficiency, but the ability to adapt rapidly to changing priorities and technologies.
SAF addresses this driver by promoting architectures that make flexibility and reuse a core principle. It supports modular designs, shared services, and scalable solutions that reduce duplication and enable more effective use of existing resources. By fostering an agile organizational mindset and clear governance around priorities, SAF allows NSIs to reallocate capacity, modernize incrementally, and continue to deliver high-quality outputs even under financial and staffing constraints.



Architecture goals represent the outcomes an organization aims to achieve by adopting and implementing aframework. They define what success looks like and serve as the link between strategy and action. In the case of the SAF, these goals are not just about modernizing IT systems, but about ensuring that national statistical institutes can continue to provide trustworthy, relevant, and high-quality statistics in a rapidly changing environment.
The goals of SAF address both operational and strategic needs. On one hand, they focus on efficiency, modernization, and compliance, which are essential for ensuring sustainability. On the other hand, they support innovation, adaptability, and collaboration, enabling statistical offices to embrace new opportunities such as integrating alternative data sources or experimenting with advanced analytics. Together, these goals ensure that modernization efforts do not compromise the fundamental values of official statistics, neutrality, accuracy, and reliability.
By defining goals explicitly, SAF provides a roadmap that can be adapted by each statistical organization according to its maturity and context. This ensures that while each office may have unique challenges and resources, they are all working toward a shared vision that promotes harmonization, comparability, and global collaboration in official statistics.



With limited budgets and growing demands, statistical organizations must operate as efficiently as possible. SAF promotes cost optimization and improved effectiveness through shared services, reuse of solutions, and stronger interoperability. By pooling resources and adopting common components, NSIs can access capabilities that would be difficult to develop individually while avoiding duplication of effort. SAF also encourages the use of open-source components and community-driven platforms where this strengthens transparency, collaboration, and cost efficiency. Through modular architectures and clear governance, organizations can adapt to changing needs, reallocate capacity, and modernize incrementally without large-scale reinvestments. This approach ensures that efficiency is achieved in ways that reinforce both quality and long-term sustainability.



Without a shared architectural reference, statistical organizations risk developing isolated solutions that reduce comparability and increase long-term costs. SAF provides a harmonized foundation of standards, patterns, and best practices that can be adapted to local contexts while supporting interoperability across borders and domains. As collaboration increasingly takes place across shared infrastructures such as national data platforms and international data spaces, harmonization also becomes a prerequisite for participation. By promoting transparency and consistent design principles, SAF helps NSIs protect the integrity of official statistics and ensure that shared and open solutions can be reused safely and effectively. A common reference framework enables collaboration, strengthens trust, and supports coherence even as the data landscape evolves.



Many statistical organizations continue to rely on fragmented and legacy IT environments that limit innovation and responsiveness. SAF provides guidance for transitioning toward modern, modular, and service-based architectures that are secure, scalable, and easier to maintain. Modernization reduces technical debt, improves reliability, and allows faster delivery of new and higher-quality statistical outputs. Modernization increasingly takes place in environments where multiple actors operate, from national infrastructures to cross-border data spaces. SAF ensures that such settings can be used safely by defining principles for access control, data protection, and accountability. It also supports a risk-based approach to automation and integration of emerging technologies. Critical processes can remain tightly governed to preserve methodological rigor, while less sensitive stages can be automated or shared.



Innovation in data and methods is central to the future of official statistics. SAF promotes an environment where experimentation, collaboration, and reuse are encouraged within secure and well-governed boundaries. By providing a clear architectural foundation, SAF enables NSIs to incorporate new data sources, tools, and analytical methods without undermining consistency or quality.
Innovation is not only about creating new solutions but also about making change possible within production. Many statistical organizations find it difficult to introduce new data sources or develop new statistical products because their production systems are optimized for predictability and stability. While these are necessary principles, they can limit agility. SAF addresses this by supporting architectures that balance robustness with flexibility, allowing new components, data, or workflows to be integrated more rapidly while maintaining full control over quality and compliance.
To make this possible, the framework emphasizes mechanisms and guardrails that enable controlled integration of innovative methods into production chains. This includes versioning, validation, and automated testing approaches that preserve reliability even as systems evolve. SAF also seeks to narrow the gap between innovation and production by promoting shared platforms and processes that allow prototypes to transition smoothly into operational environments.
Open source plays a key role in this innovation process. It allows organizations to build on each other’s work, increase transparency, and strengthen the collective capacity of the statistical community. SAF supports this through architectural patterns that enable safe reuse of open components and integration with shared platforms. In doing so, it helps turn innovation into a structured, sustainable part of statistical production.



Compliance with regulations, standards, and ethical principles is fundamental to maintaining the trust and legitimacy of official statistics. SAF ensures that modernization aligns with legal, security, and quality frameworks while promoting transparency and accountability. Within the statistical domain, well-established standards such as GSBPM, GSIM, and SDMX continue to provide a foundation for consistent processes, metadata management, and data exchange. These remain essential for ensuring methodological rigor and comparability across the statistical system.
However, as the production of statistics becomes increasingly integrated into the broader data and technology ecosystem, compliance must also extend beyond traditional statistical standards. SAF encourages active engagement with and adoption of relevant standards from adjacent fields such as data management, artificial intelligence, and cloud computing. This outward-looking approach ensures that NSIs remain interoperable with modern data platforms and can benefit from technological progress developed outside the statistical community.
Through consistent governance and the use of open, verifiable technologies, SAF supports compliance as an enabler rather than a constraint. It provides the structures necessary to ensure that innovation, data sharing, and open collaboration occur within controlled and auditable environments. This approach reinforces public trust by embedding transparency, scientific rigor, and privacy-by-design across all processes.




Architecture meaning provides the “why” behind the framework. While goals and outcomes describe what SAF achieves, meaning explains why it matters. For statistical organizations, architecture is not just a technical exercise but a way of ensuring their continued relevance in a digital society. SAF’s meaning lies in its role as the foundation for modernization, trust, and international collaboration.

One dimension of this meaning is its role as a bridge between strategy and technology. Without such a framework, investments in IT risk being disconnected from the mission of providing high-quality statistics. SAF ensures that every technological decision, from adopting a new platform to restructuring business processes, can be traced back to strategic objectives, creating a coherent organizational narrative.
Another dimension is collaboration. The meaning of SAF extends beyond individual organizations: it is a unifying language for the UNECE statistical community. By providing shared models, practices, and principles, SAF fosters international collaboration, reduces duplication, and amplifies collective impact. In this sense, SAF is not just meaningful to IT professionals but to the broader community of statisticians, policymakers, and citizens who depend on trustworthy statistics.



SAF connects high-level strategic objectives, such as improving statistical relevance and efficiency, with concrete technology choices. It ensures that IT investments are always justified by their contribution to the organization’s mission.



SAF is a unifying framework for the statistical community. It enables organizations to work together on shared goals, whether through joint platforms, interoperable systems, or harmonized standards, thereby amplifying the collective capacity of UNECE members.



SAF is not just a set of technical models; it is the foundation for digital transformation in official statistics. It enables NSIs to embrace innovation without sacrificing methodological rigor or institutional trust.



By adopting TOGAF and ArchiMate, SAF ensures that diverse stakeholders can communicate using a consistent language and notation. This reduces misunderstandings, enables shared modelling practices, and promotes architectural maturity across the community.
